claim: The signal recognition particle (SRP) directs translating ribosome-nascent chain complexes (RNCs) that display a signal sequence to protein translocation channels in target membranes.
source: The signal recognition particle (SRP) directs translating ribosome-nascent chain complexes (RNCs) that display a signal sequence to protein translocation channels in target membranes.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by extensive prior research.

claim: All previous work on the initial step of the targeting reaction used stalled and non-translating RNCs.
source: All previous work on the initial step of the targeting reaction, when SRP binds to RNCs, used stalled and non-translating RNCs.
evidence: This statement characterizes the state of prior research in the field.

claim: At physiologically relevant SRP concentrations, SRP-RNC association and dissociation rates depend on nascent chain length and the exposure of a functional signal sequence outside the ribosome.
source: We show at physiologically relevant SRP concentrations that SRP-RNC association and dissociation rates depend on nascent chain length and the exposure of a functional signal sequence outside the ribosome.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the figures.

claim: SRP only stably engages translating RNCs exposing a functional signal sequence.
source: The answer is strikingly simple: as originally proposed, SRP only stably engages translating RNCs exposing a functional signal sequence.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the experimental data showing delayed first SRP binding and dependence on signal sequence exposure.

claim: SRP in all three kingdoms of life catalyzes the co-translational targeting of membrane and secretory proteins.
source: The signal recognition particle (SRP) in all three kingdoms of life catalyzes the co-translational targeting of membrane and secretory proteins (Egea et al., 2005; Zhang and Shan, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: At the beginning of the targeting reaction, SRP binds to a ribosome-nascent chain complex (RNC).
source: At the beginning of the targeting reaction, SRP binds to a ribosome-nascent chain complex (RNC).
evidence: This is a well-established step in the SRP targeting pathway.

claim: If the RNC displays a signal sequence, RNC-bound SRP binds the SRP receptor at the target membrane.
source: If the RNC displays a signal sequence, RNC-bound SRP binds the SRP receptor at the target membrane (the endoplasmic reticulum membrane in eukaryotes, or the inner membrane in prokaryotes).
evidence: This describes the subsequent step in the SRP targeting pathway.

claim: The membrane-localized RNC is transferred to the translocon, a protein translocation channel through which the nascent chain passes across, or into, the target membrane.
source: The membrane-localized RNC is then transferred to the translocon, a protein translocation channel through which the nascent chain passes across, or into, the target membrane.
evidence: This describes the final step in the SRP targeting pathway.

claim: Mammalian SRP is composed of a 300-nucleotide RNA and 6 protein subunits.
source: Whereas mammalian SRP is composed of a 300-nucleotide RNA and 6 protein subunits, the simpler Escherichia coli SRP is composed of a 114-nucleotide RNA (4.5S RNA) homologous to a conserved domain of the eukaryotic SRP RNA and a single protein subunit (Ffh), a homolog of the mammalian SRP54 subunit.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition of mammalian SRP.

claim: E. coli SRP is composed of a 114-nucleotide RNA (4.5S RNA) and a single protein subunit (Ffh).
source: Whereas mammalian SRP is composed of a 300-nucleotide RNA and 6 protein subunits, the simpler Escherichia coli SRP is composed of a 114-nucleotide RNA (4.5S RNA) homologous to a conserved domain of the eukaryotic SRP RNA and a single protein subunit (Ffh), a homolog of the mammalian SRP54 subunit.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition of E. coli SRP.

claim: E. coli 4.5S RNA is homologous to a conserved domain of the eukaryotic SRP RNA.
source: Whereas mammalian SRP is composed of a 300-nucleotide RNA and 6 protein subunits, the simpler Escherichia coli SRP is composed of a 114-nucleotide RNA (4.5S RNA) homologous to a conserved domain of the eukaryotic SRP RNA and a single protein subunit (Ffh), a homolog of the mammalian SRP54 subunit.
evidence: This describes the evolutionary relationship between bacterial and eukaryotic SRP components.

claim: E. coli Ffh is a homolog of the mammalian SRP54 subunit.
source: Whereas mammalian SRP is composed of a 300-nucleotide RNA and 6 protein subunits, the simpler Escherichia coli SRP is composed of a 114-nucleotide RNA (4.5S RNA) homologous to a conserved domain of the eukaryotic SRP RNA and a single protein subunit (Ffh), a homolog of the mammalian SRP54 subunit.
evidence: This describes the evolutionary relationship between bacterial and eukaryotic SRP components.

claim: E. coli SRP can efficiently replace mammalian SRP in in vitro targeting reactions.
source: The E. coli SRP, which is used in these studies, can efficiently replace mammalian SRP in in vitro targeting reactions, demonstrating that it retains the core targeting functionality (Bernstein et al., 1993; Powers and Walter, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: E. coli SRP retains the core targeting functionality of mammalian SRP.
source: The E. coli SRP, which is used in these studies, can efficiently replace mammalian SRP in in vitro targeting reactions, demonstrating that it retains the core targeting functionality (Bernstein et al., 1993; Powers and Walter, 1997).
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of E. coli SRP to replace mammalian SRP functionally.

claim: Equilibrium measurements of SRP binding affinities to RNCs stalled with nascent chains up to 35 amino acids in length indicated very tight binding (∼1–100 nM binding constants).
source: Equilibrium measurements of SRP binding affinities to RNCs stalled with nascent chains up to 35 amino acids in length indicated very tight binding (∼1–100 nM binding constants) (Bornemann et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: At any given moment, approximately 10% of RNCs have a nascent chain less than 35 amino acids long.
source: An estimate based on ribosome profiling of the ∼2000 most expressed proteins in E. coli indicates that at any given moment ∼10% of RNCs have a nascent chain less than 35 amino acids long (Oh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to ribosome profiling data.

claim: The SRP concentration in E. coli is approximately 400 nM.
source: Considering that the SRP concentration in E. coli is ∼400 nM (100-fold less than the ribosomal concentration) (Jensen and Pedersen, 1994), such tight binding affinities would result in 75–100% of the SRP to be bound to these RNCs that are not exposing a signal sequence, and the majority of which (∼95%) never will (Bornemann et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior measurements.

claim: The SRP concentration in E. coli is 100-fold less than the ribosomal concentration.
source: Considering that the SRP concentration in E. coli is ∼400 nM (100-fold less than the ribosomal concentration) (Jensen and Pedersen, 1994), such tight binding affinities would result in 75–100% of the SRP to be bound to these RNCs that are not exposing a signal sequence, and the majority of which (∼95%) never will (Bornemann et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the stated SRP concentration and ribosome concentration.

claim: Tight SRP binding affinities to short nascent chains would result in 75–100% of the SRP being bound to RNCs not exposing a signal sequence.
source: Considering that the SRP concentration in E. coli is ∼400 nM (100-fold less than the ribosomal concentration) (Jensen and Pedersen, 1994), such tight binding affinities would result in 75–100% of the SRP to be bound to these RNCs that are not exposing a signal sequence, and the majority of which (∼95%) never will (Bornemann et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the cited binding affinities and cellular concentrations.

claim: Approximately 95% of RNCs with nascent chains less than 35 amino acids will never expose a signal sequence.
source: Considering that the SRP concentration in E. coli is ∼400 nM (100-fold less than the ribosomal concentration) (Jensen and Pedersen, 1994), such tight binding affinities would result in 75–100% of the SRP to be bound to these RNCs that are not exposing a signal sequence, and the majority of which (∼95%) never will (Bornemann et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: SRP binding to RNCs without signal sequences would result in a large unproductive sink on the targeting reaction.
source: SRP binding to these RNCs would thus result in a large unproductive sink on the targeting reaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the previous calculations about SRP binding to non-signal sequence RNCs.

claim: Regardless of nascent chain length, SRP arrives at RNCs very quickly with arrival rates on the order of 10^6 M^−1 sec^−1.
source: Kinetic studies attempted to resolve this issue and concluded that, regardless of nascent chain length, SRP arrives at RNCs very quickly (arrival rates on the order of 106 M−1 sec−1) and that nascent chain length mostly affects dissociation rates (although different studies have determined a wide range of dissociation rates: ∼10–0.01 s−1 for RNCs with no nascent chain and ∼0.1 to 2 × 10−4 s−1 for RNCs with an exposed signal sequence) (Holtkamp et al., 2012; Noriega et al., 2014; Saraogi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior kinetic studies.

claim: Nascent chain length mostly affects SRP-RNC dissociation rates.
source: Kinetic studies attempted to resolve this issue and concluded that, regardless of nascent chain length, SRP arrives at RNCs very quickly (arrival rates on the order of 106 M−1 sec−1) and that nascent chain length mostly affects dissociation rates (although different studies have determined a wide range of dissociation rates: ∼10–0.01 s−1 for RNCs with no nascent chain and ∼0.1 to 2 × 10−4 s−1 for RNCs with an exposed signal sequence) (Holtkamp et al., 2012; Noriega et al., 2014; Saraogi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior kinetic studies.

claim: Different studies have determined a wide range of SRP-RNC dissociation rates: approximately 10–0.01 s^−1 for RNCs with no nascent chain and approximately 0.1 to 2 × 10^−4 s^−1 for RNCs with an exposed signal sequence.
source: Kinetic studies attempted to resolve this issue and concluded that, regardless of nascent chain length, SRP arrives at RNCs very quickly (arrival rates on the order of 106 M−1 sec−1) and that nascent chain length mostly affects dissociation rates (although different studies have determined a wide range of dissociation rates: ∼10–0.01 s−1 for RNCs with no nascent chain and ∼0.1 to 2 × 10−4 s−1 for RNCs with an exposed signal sequence) (Holtkamp et al., 2012; Noriega et al., 2014; Saraogi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior kinetic studies.

claim: SRP non-specifically and quickly arrives to RNCs as soon as they begin translating and remains bound until a nascent chain without a signal sequence becomes long enough to emerge from the ribosomal peptide tunnel and sterically displace SRP.
source: The models that emerged had SRP non-specifically, and quickly arriving to RNCs as soon they begin translating and remaining bound until a nascent chain without a signal sequence becomes long enough to emerge from the ribosomal peptide tunnel and sterically displace SRP.
evidence: This describes a model proposed in prior work based on kinetic studies.

claim: An additional factor such as the co-translational chaperone trigger factor was proposed to bind the RNC and displace SRP.
source: Alternatively, the possibility of an additional factor (such as the co-translational chaperone trigger factor) was proposed to bind the RNC and displace SRP (Holtkamp et al., 2012; Bornemann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work proposing this alternative model.

claim: In either model, a large pool of SRP would be unproductively bound for a significant amount of time until displaced.
source: In either model, a large pool of SRP would be unproductively bound for a significant amount of time until displaced.
evidence: This is inferred from the models described in prior work.

claim: Prior studies of SRP-RNC binding were performed on RNCs that had been stalled while translating the nascent chain.
source: Prior studies of SRP-RNC binding were performed on RNCs that had been stalled while translating the nascent chain.
evidence: This characterizes the methodology of prior studies.

claim: The stalled RNC approach was technically necessary to create homogenous RNC populations.
source: This approach was technically necessary to create homogenous RNC populations, but lacked the key temporal dimension, provided by active translation by RNCs.
evidence: This explains the rationale for using stalled RNCs in prior studies.

claim: The stalled RNC approach lacked the key temporal dimension provided by active translation by RNCs.
source: This approach was technically necessary to create homogenous RNC populations, but lacked the key temporal dimension, provided by active translation by RNCs.
evidence: This is a critique of prior methodology.

claim: Multiple parameters are dynamically changing during active translation: ribosome conformations, nascent chain composition, and length and folding state of the chain outside the ribosomal peptide tunnel.
source: Multiple parameters are dynamically changing during active translation: (i) ribosome conformations, which cycle through pre- and post-elongation states, (ii) nascent chain composition, which changes with each new amino acid added, (iii) and length and folding state of the chain outside the ribosomal peptide tunnel.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of translation dynamics.

claim: Ribosome conformations cycle through pre- and post-elongation states during active translation.
source: Multiple parameters are dynamically changing during active translation: (i) ribosome conformations, which cycle through pre- and post-elongation states, (ii) nascent chain composition, which changes with each new amino acid added, (iii) and length and folding state of the chain outside the ribosomal peptide tunnel.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of ribosome dynamics.

claim: Nascent chain composition changes with each new amino acid added during active translation.
source: Multiple parameters are dynamically changing during active translation: (i) ribosome conformations, which cycle through pre- and post-elongation states, (ii) nascent chain composition, which changes with each new amino acid added, (iii) and length and folding state of the chain outside the ribosomal peptide tunnel.
evidence: This is a basic fact about translation.

claim: These factors could affect how SRP interacts with and subsequently targets translating RNCs.
source: These factors all could affect how SRP interacts with, and subsequently targets, the translating RNCs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the potential effects of translation dynamics on SRP-RNC interactions.

claim: A single-molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer (smFRET) assay was developed to observe SRP binding to actively translating RNCs at physiologically relevant SRP concentrations.
source: Here we developed a single-molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer (smFRET) assay that allowed us to observe SRP binding to actively translating RNCs at physiologically relevant SRP concentrations.
evidence: This describes the methodology developed in this study.

claim: Both association and dissociation rates of SRP binding are sensitive to active RNC translation.
source: We show that both association and dissociation rates of SRP binding are sensitive to active RNC translation, with rapid and stable SRP binding to RNCs only upon exposure of a signal sequence outside the ribosomal peptide tunnel.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Rapid and stable SRP binding to RNCs occurs only upon exposure of a signal sequence outside the ribosomal peptide tunnel.
source: We show that both association and dissociation rates of SRP binding are sensitive to active RNC translation, with rapid and stable SRP binding to RNCs only upon exposure of a signal sequence outside the ribosomal peptide tunnel.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The 50S ribosome subunit was labeled with the FRET donor dye Cy3B at a unique cysteine on ribosomal protein L29.
source: To this end, we labeled the 50S ribosome subunit with the FRET donor dye Cy3B at a unique cysteine on ribosomal protein L29 (Noriega et al., 2014) and, analogously, SRP with the FRET acceptor dye Cy5 at a unique cysteine in the NG domain of Ffh (Zhang et al., 2008; Shen et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology with citation to prior work.

claim: SRP was labeled with the FRET acceptor dye Cy5 at a unique cysteine in the NG domain of Ffh.
source: To this end, we labeled the 50S ribosome subunit with the FRET donor dye Cy3B at a unique cysteine on ribosomal protein L29 (Noriega et al., 2014) and, analogously, SRP with the FRET acceptor dye Cy5 at a unique cysteine in the NG domain of Ffh (Zhang et al., 2008; Shen et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology with citation to prior work.

claim: According to all structurally characterized SRP-RNC conformations, the dye positions have inter-dye distances within approximately 40 and 50 Å.
source: According to all structurally characterized SRP-RNC conformations, these dye positions have inter-dye distances within ∼40 and 50 Å (Halic et al., 2006; Schaffitzel et al., 2006), allowing for detectable FRET between SRP and the ribosome given that the Forster radius of the dyes is ∼65 Å (Uphoff et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on structural data from prior studies.

claim: The Forster radius of the Cy3B-Cy5 dye pair is approximately 65 Å.
source: According to all structurally characterized SRP-RNC conformations, these dye positions have inter-dye distances within ∼40 and 50 Å (Halic et al., 2006; Schaffitzel et al., 2006), allowing for detectable FRET between SRP and the ribosome given that the Forster radius of the dyes is ∼65 Å (Uphoff et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a known property of the dye pair, supported by citation.

claim: The dye positions allow for detectable FRET between SRP and the ribosome.
source: According to all structurally characterized SRP-RNC conformations, these dye positions have inter-dye distances within ∼40 and 50 Å (Halic et al., 2006; Schaffitzel et al., 2006), allowing for detectable FRET between SRP and the ribosome given that the Forster radius of the dyes is ∼65 Å (Uphoff et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the inter-dye distances and Forster radius.

claim: smFRET experiments were performed using zero-mode waveguides (ZMWs) to observe SRP binding at relevant concentrations.
source: To observe SRP binding at relevant concentrations, we performed smFRET experiments using zero-mode waveguides (ZMWs), in which fluorescence measurements are taken from reactions occurring within small metallic apertures (∼150 nm in diameter) that are patterned onto a glass substrate (Chen et al., 2014a).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: ZMWs are small metallic apertures approximately 150 nm in diameter patterned onto a glass substrate.
source: To observe SRP binding at relevant concentrations, we performed smFRET experiments using zero-mode waveguides (ZMWs), in which fluorescence measurements are taken from reactions occurring within small metallic apertures (∼150 nm in diameter) that are patterned onto a glass substrate (Chen et al., 2014a).
evidence: This describes the physical properties of ZMWs with citation to prior work.

claim: ZMWs limit background fluorescence from labeled reaction components in solution.
source: ZMWs limit background fluorescence from labeled reaction components in solution, which allowed us to measure SRP-RNC binding at 100 nM Cy5-labeled SRP, which is very close to the physiological 400 nM SRP concentration in bacterial cells (Jensen and Pedersen, 1994).
evidence: This describes the advantage of using ZMWs for these experiments.

claim: ZMWs allowed measurement of SRP-RNC binding at 100 nM Cy5-labeled SRP, which is very close to the physiological 400 nM SRP concentration in bacterial cells.
source: ZMWs limit background fluorescence from labeled reaction components in solution, which allowed us to measure SRP-RNC binding at 100 nM Cy5-labeled SRP, which is very close to the physiological 400 nM SRP concentration in bacterial cells (Jensen and Pedersen, 1994).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions and their physiological relevance.

claim: LepB is a well-characterized in vivo SRP substrate with an N-terminal signal sequence.
source: LepB is a well-characterized in vivo SRP substrate with an N-terminal signal sequence (de Gier et al., 1996; Bornemann et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A 3′-truncated lepB mRNA encoding the first 155 amino acids was immobilized via a biotinylated linker on ZMWs.
source: A 3′-truncated lepB mRNA encoding the first 155 amino acids was immobilized via a biotinylated linker on ZMWs.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: Pre-initiation complexes (PICs) are composed of 30S ribosomal subunit, formylated methionine-tRNAfMet, and initiation factor 2 in complex with GTP.
source: Pre-initiation complexes ('PICs'; composed of 30S ribosomal subunit, formylated methionine-tRNAfMet, and initiation factor 2 in complex with GTP) were then assembled on the mRNA.
evidence: This describes the composition of PICs based on established knowledge.

claim: On average, the first SRP binding events were much delayed (approximately 50-fold) compared to subsequent events.
source: This analysis showed that on average the first SRP binding events were much delayed (∼50-fold), compared to subsequent events (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The time-dependent progression from a period of no SRP-RNC binding events to one of multiple SRP-RNC binding events is consistent with the original conception of SRP function.
source: The time-dependent progression from a period of no SRP-RNC binding events to one of multiple SRP-RNC binding events is consistent with the original conception of SRP function, which posed that SRP only effectively binds RNCs after the signal sequence on the nascent chain emerged from the ribosomal peptide tunnel (Walter et al., 1981).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by the experimental data and citation to the original proposal.

claim: The original conception of SRP function posed that SRP only effectively binds RNCs after the signal sequence on the nascent chain emerged from the ribosomal peptide tunnel.
source: The time-dependent progression from a period of no SRP-RNC binding events to one of multiple SRP-RNC binding events is consistent with the original conception of SRP function, which posed that SRP only effectively binds RNCs after the signal sequence on the nascent chain emerged from the ribosomal peptide tunnel (Walter et al., 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original work.

claim: Elongation rate is directly related to EF-G concentration.
source: Since elongation rate is directly related to EF-G concentration, RNCs will translate the lepB mRNA more slowly at lower EF-G concentration.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of translation mechanics.

claim: RNCs translate the lepB mRNA more slowly at lower EF-G concentration.
source: Since elongation rate is directly related to EF-G concentration, RNCs will translate the lepB mRNA more slowly at lower EF-G concentration.
evidence: This is inferred from the relationship between EF-G concentration and elongation rate.

claim: As RNCs translate more slowly, it takes longer for the signal sequence to become available.
source: We predicted that as RNCs translate more slowly, it would take longer for the signal sequence to become available and hence make observation of multiple SRP binding events during the recorded time course less likely (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on translation dynamics.

claim: Slower translation makes observation of multiple SRP binding events during the recorded time course less likely.
source: We predicted that as RNCs translate more slowly, it would take longer for the signal sequence to become available and hence make observation of multiple SRP binding events during the recorded time course less likely (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on translation dynamics.

claim: Approximately 50% of RNCs had more than two SRP binding events in reactions containing 250 nM EF-G.
source: Indeed, we observed fewer SRP binding events per RNC at the lower EF-G concentration: ∼50% of RNCs had more than two SRP binding events in reactions containing 250 nM EF-G, whereas ∼80% of RNCs had more than two SRP binding events in reactions containing 750 nM EF-G (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Approximately 80% of RNCs had more than two SRP binding events in reactions containing 750 nM EF-G.
source: Indeed, we observed fewer SRP binding events per RNC at the lower EF-G concentration: ∼50% of RNCs had more than two SRP binding events in reactions containing 250 nM EF-G, whereas ∼80% of RNCs had more than two SRP binding events in reactions containing 750 nM EF-G (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The half-time of first SRP arrival was approximately 350 s in 250 nM EF-G reactions.
source: Moreover, as expected, the initial SRP-RNC binding events occurred later at lower EF-G concentrations: the half-time of first arrival was ∼350 s in 250 nM EF-G reactions and ∼280 s in 750 nM EF-G reactions (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The half-time of first SRP arrival was approximately 280 s in 750 nM EF-G reactions.
source: Moreover, as expected, the initial SRP-RNC binding events occurred later at lower EF-G concentrations: the half-time of first arrival was ∼350 s in 250 nM EF-G reactions and ∼280 s in 750 nM EF-G reactions (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The half-time of subsequent SRP arrivals was approximately 12 s in 250 nM EF-G reactions.
source: SRP arrival events that followed the initial binding event were similarly slower at the lower EF-G concentrations: half-time of arrival was ∼12 s in 250 nM EF-G reactions and ∼5 s in 750 nM EF-G reactions (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The half-time of subsequent SRP arrivals was approximately 5 s in 750 nM EF-G reactions.
source: SRP arrival events that followed the initial binding event were similarly slower at the lower EF-G concentrations: half-time of arrival was ∼12 s in 250 nM EF-G reactions and ∼5 s in 750 nM EF-G reactions (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: It takes slowly elongating RNCs longer to translate nascent chains in which the signal sequence is optimally exposed, allowing SRP to bind most effectively.
source: These latter results are explained because it takes slowly elongating RNCs longer to translate nascent chains in which the signal sequence is optimally exposed, allowing SRP to bind most effectively (Noriega et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data with citation to prior work.

claim: Translation rates under single-molecule conditions are approximately 5–10 s per amino acid at the elongation factor concentrations used.
source: From previous calibrations of translation rates under single-molecule conditions (∼5–10 s per amino acid, at the elongation factor concentrations used) (Uemura et al., 2010), we estimate that the first SRP arrival times occurred after approximately 35–45 amino acids were polymerized.
evidence: This is based on citation to prior calibration work.

claim: The first SRP arrival times occurred after approximately 35–45 amino acids were polymerized.
source: From previous calibrations of translation rates under single-molecule conditions (∼5–10 s per amino acid, at the elongation factor concentrations used) (Uemura et al., 2010), we estimate that the first SRP arrival times occurred after approximately 35–45 amino acids were polymerized.
evidence: This is an estimate based on translation rate calibrations and observed arrival times.

claim: A nascent chain length of 35–45 amino acids corresponds to the partial emergence of a signal sequence from the ribosome.
source: This nascent chain length would correspond to the partial emergence of a signal sequence from the ribosome (Houben et al., 2005; Bornemann et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on signal sequence emergence.

claim: An engineered 3′-end truncated lepB mRNA encoding 95 amino acids was used to calibrate the extent of translation.
source: To this end, we used an engineered 3′-end truncated lepB mRNA encoding 95 amino acids.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The calibration mRNA contained a single phenylalanine codon followed by three clusters of three sequential phenylalanine codons as chain length markers at positions 5, 25–27, 55–57, and 85–87.
source: The mRNA contained a single phenylalanine codon followed by three clusters of three sequential phenylalanine codons as chain length markers at positions 5, 25–27, 55–57, and 85–87 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, cWT for 'calibration WT').
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Pulses in Cy3.5 fluorescence intensity were observed when phenylalanine was incorporated into the nascent chain.
source: After replacing unlabeled phenylalanine tRNA (tRNAPhe) in the translation mix with Cy3.5-labeled tRNAPhe and monitoring Cy3.5 fluorescence, we observed pulses in fluorescence intensity when phenylalanine was incorporated into the nascent chain (Chen et al., 2014b; Tsai et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the experimental observation with citation to prior work using similar methods.

claim: The duration of the tRNA pulses represents the transit of tRNAPhe through two rounds of peptide elongation and departure.
source: The duration of the pulses represent the transit of tRNAPhe through two rounds of peptide elongation and departure, whereas interpulse durations represent the translation time between the phenylalanine codons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pulse durations based on knowledge of translation mechanics.

claim: Interpulse durations represent the translation time between the phenylalanine codons.
source: The duration of the pulses represent the transit of tRNAPhe through two rounds of peptide elongation and departure, whereas interpulse durations represent the translation time between the phenylalanine codons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the interpulse durations based on knowledge of translation mechanics.

claim: The majority of RNC traces that showed SRP binding displayed three or four tRNAPhe pulses.
source: The tRNAPhe pulses behaved as expected: (i) The majority of RNC traces that showed SRP binding displayed three or four tRNAPhe pulses (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, upper left panel);
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The second, third, and fourth tRNA pulses showed the same average lifetimes (approximately 30 s).
source: (ii) the second, third, and fourth tRNA pulses, during which clusters of three phenylalanines were incorporated, showed the same average lifetimes (∼30 s) and lasted three-times longer than the average lifetime of the first pulse (∼10 s), in which only a single phenylalanine was incorporated (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, upper right panel);
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The second, third, and fourth tRNA pulses lasted three-times longer than the average lifetime of the first pulse.
source: (ii) the second, third, and fourth tRNA pulses, during which clusters of three phenylalanines were incorporated, showed the same average lifetimes (∼30 s) and lasted three-times longer than the average lifetime of the first pulse (∼10 s), in which only a single phenylalanine was incorporated (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, upper right panel);
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The first tRNA pulse had an average lifetime of approximately 10 s.
source: (ii) the second, third, and fourth tRNA pulses, during which clusters of three phenylalanines were incorporated, showed the same average lifetimes (∼30 s) and lasted three-times longer than the average lifetime of the first pulse (∼10 s), in which only a single phenylalanine was incorporated (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, upper right panel);
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The inter-pulse times were proportional to the number of codons translated between them.
source: and (iii) the inter-pulse times were proportional to the number of codons translated between them (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, lower panels).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The RNCs under the assay conditions are actively translating.
source: These results indicate that the RNCs under our assay conditions are actively translating and that we can accurately calibrate the reaction to map SRP binding events on nascent chain length.
evidence: This is inferred from the tRNA pulse behavior matching expectations for active translation.

claim: The reaction can be accurately calibrated to map SRP binding events on nascent chain length.
source: These results indicate that the RNCs under our assay conditions are actively translating and that we can accurately calibrate the reaction to map SRP binding events on nascent chain length.
evidence: This is inferred from the tRNA pulse behavior matching expectations.

claim: The majority of first SRP-RNC binding events (68%) occurred when RNCs had translated between 40 and 55 amino acids.
source: We observed that the majority of first binding events occurred when RNCs had translated between 40 and 55 amino acids (68% of all events) (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), corresponding to a nascent chain length at which the signal sequence emerges from the ribosomal peptide tunnel (Houben et al., 2005; Bornemann et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A nascent chain length of 40-55 amino acids corresponds to when the signal sequence emerges from the ribosomal peptide tunnel.
source: We observed that the majority of first binding events occurred when RNCs had translated between 40 and 55 amino acids (68% of all events) (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), corresponding to a nascent chain length at which the signal sequence emerges from the ribosomal peptide tunnel (Houben et al., 2005; Bornemann et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on signal sequence emergence.

claim: Only 9% of observed first SRP arrivals occurred before the nascent chain was 40 amino acids long.
source: Only 9% of observed first arrivals occurred before the nascent chain was 40 amino acids long.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data.

claim: A mutated lepB signal sequence was previously shown to be inactive.
source: To confirm the dependence of SRP-RNC binding on the presence of a functional signal sequence, we measured SRP binding in a reaction translating lepB with a mutated signal sequence, previously shown to be inactive (Houben et al., 2005) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, cMT for 'calibration mutant').
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: SRP binding events were virtually absent upon translation of the cMT lepB mRNA with mutated signal sequence.
source: SRP binding events were virtually absent upon translation of the cMT lepB mRNA (Figure 3C,E).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 3C and 3E.

claim: Past a 50 amino acid nascent chain length, SRP-RNC binding events occurred in quick succession at a rate of 1 per approximately 1–2 codons translated.
source: We also observed that, past a 50 amino acid nascent chain length, SRP-RNC binding events occurred in quick succession (at a rate of 1 per ∼1–2 codons translated after 50 amino acid chain length, as opposed to 1 per ∼50 codons before 50 amino acid chain length) (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), consistent with the ∼50-fold increase in SRP association rates upon exposure of a functional signal sequence shown above in Figure 1B.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data.

claim: Before 50 amino acid nascent chain length, SRP-RNC binding events occurred at a rate of 1 per approximately 50 codons translated.
source: We also observed that, past a 50 amino acid nascent chain length, SRP-RNC binding events occurred in quick succession (at a rate of 1 per ∼1–2 codons translated after 50 amino acid chain length, as opposed to 1 per ∼50 codons before 50 amino acid chain length) (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), consistent with the ∼50-fold increase in SRP association rates upon exposure of a functional signal sequence shown above in Figure 1B.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data.

claim: The change in SRP binding event frequency is consistent with the approximately 50-fold increase in SRP association rates upon exposure of a functional signal sequence.
source: We also observed that, past a 50 amino acid nascent chain length, SRP-RNC binding events occurred in quick succession (at a rate of 1 per ∼1–2 codons translated after 50 amino acid chain length, as opposed to 1 per ∼50 codons before 50 amino acid chain length) (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), consistent with the ∼50-fold increase in SRP association rates upon exposure of a functional signal sequence shown above in Figure 1B.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting different experimental observations.

claim: SRP-RNC residence times were dependent on translation.
source: We also observed that SRP-RNC residence times were dependent on translation.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Residence times were longest when RNCs were translating nascent chains in the 50–60 amino acid range with average lifetimes of 74.4 ± 5.0 s.
source: Residence times were longest when RNCs were translating nascent chains in the 50–60 amino acid range (Figure 3C, red squares and dashed line; average lifetimes of 74.4 ± 5.0 s).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Shorter or longer nascent chain lengths resulted in approximately two-fold briefer SRP-RNC residence times.
source: Shorter or longer nascent chain lengths resulted in ∼two-fold briefer SRP-RNC residence times (Figure 3C, red squares and dashed line; average lifetimes of 34.7 ± 4.1 and 37.8 ± 3.5 s for chains in the 40–50 and 60–70 amino acid range, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Average SRP-RNC residence times for chains in the 40–50 amino acid range were 34.7 ± 4.1 s.
source: Shorter or longer nascent chain lengths resulted in ∼two-fold briefer SRP-RNC residence times (Figure 3C, red squares and dashed line; average lifetimes of 34.7 ± 4.1 and 37.8 ± 3.5 s for chains in the 40–50 and 60–70 amino acid range, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Average SRP-RNC residence times for chains in the 60–70 amino acid range were 37.8 ± 3.5 s.
source: Shorter or longer nascent chain lengths resulted in ∼two-fold briefer SRP-RNC residence times (Figure 3C, red squares and dashed line; average lifetimes of 34.7 ± 4.1 and 37.8 ± 3.5 s for chains in the 40–50 and 60–70 amino acid range, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The residence time results are consistent with SRP binding most effectively (with the longest residence time) to nascent chains of an optimal length.
source: These results are consistent with SRP binding most effectively (with the longest residence time) to nascent chains of an optimal length (Noriega et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data with citation to prior work.

claim: As nascent chains grew from 45 to 60 amino acids, a rapid increase in the RNC occupancy by SRP was observed.
source: As nascent chains grew from 45 to 60 amino acids, we observed a rapid increase in the RNC occupancy by SRP (where occupancy refers to the number of RNCs that are bound by SRP, with RNCs grouped by amino acids translated) (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 4), which depended on a functional signal sequence.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The increase in RNC occupancy by SRP depended on a functional signal sequence.
source: As nascent chains grew from 45 to 60 amino acids, we observed a rapid increase in the RNC occupancy by SRP (where occupancy refers to the number of RNCs that are bound by SRP, with RNCs grouped by amino acids translated) (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 4), which depended on a functional signal sequence.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: When the signal sequence was mutated, SRP occupancy was lost.
source: When the signal sequence was mutated, occupancy was lost.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data comparing wild-type and mutant signal sequences.

claim: The results establish a new experimental paradigm in which the association of numerous other factors that interact co-translationally with RNCs can be characterized dynamically.
source: The results presented here establish a new experimental paradigm in which the association of numerous other factors that interact co-translationally with RNCs, such as chaperones and nascent chain modifying enzymes, can be characterized dynamically.
evidence: This is a broader implication of the methodology developed in this study.

claim: SRP does not engage stably with translating RNCs that do not expose a functional signal sequence.
source: Our results suggest that SRP does not engage stably with translating RNCs that do not expose a functional signal sequence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The results are consistent with past biochemical and structural work showing that SRP can directly bind to an exposed signal sequence.
source: These results are consistent with past biochemical and structural work showing that SRP can directly bind to an exposed signal sequence (Zopf et al., 1990; Keenan et al., 1998; Janda et al., 2010).
evidence: This connects the current findings to prior work through citations.

claim: The conclusions contrast with those of previous work on stalled ribosomes, which suggested that SRP can bind prominently to RNCs with nascent chains as short as 20 amino acids containing a signal sequence still occluded within the ribosome.
source: However, the conclusions contrast with those of previous work on stalled ribosomes, which suggested that SRP can bind prominently to RNCs with nascent chains as short as 20 amino acids containing a signal sequence still occluded within the ribosome (Bornemann et al., 2008; Holtkamp et al., 2012).
evidence: This contrasts the current findings with prior work through citations.

claim: The kinetic parameter most responsible for the observed signal sequence discrimination is a highly variable SRP-RNC association rate.
source: We determined that the kinetic parameter most responsible for the observed signal sequence discrimination is a highly variable SRP-RNC association rate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: When no signal sequence is exposed on RNCs, the SRP association rate is greater than 3.5 × 10^4 M^−1 s^−1 for experiments performed at 750 nM EF-G.
source: When no signal sequence is exposed on RNCs (>3.5 × 104 M−1 s−1, for the experiments performed at 750 nM EF-G), we observed only negligible SRP occupancy.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data.

claim: When no signal sequence is exposed on RNCs, only negligible SRP occupancy was observed.
source: When no signal sequence is exposed on RNCs (>3.5 × 104 M−1 s−1, for the experiments performed at 750 nM EF-G), we observed only negligible SRP occupancy.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: After translation advances far enough to have a signal sequence exposed on an RNC, the SRP association rates become at least 50-fold faster (approximately 1.8 × 10^6 M^−1 s^−1 for experiments performed at 750 nM EF-G).
source: After translation advances far enough to have a signal sequence exposed on an RNC, the SRP association rates become at least 50-fold faster (∼1.8 × 106 M−1 s−1, for the experiments performed at 750 nM EF-G).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data.

claim: The current results contrast with previous work suggesting that stable SRP-RNC complex association rates are insensitive to nascent chain length.
source: This contrasts with previous work suggesting that stable SRP-RNC complex association rates are insensitive to nascent chain length (Holtkamp et al., 2012; Saraogi et al., 2014).
evidence: This contrasts the current findings with prior work through citations.

claim: The system is based on a FRET signal between dyes on the ribosome and SRP, limiting detection to interactions in which the inter-dye distance is less than approximately 95 Å.
source: Our system is based on a FRET signal between dyes on the ribosome and SRP, limiting detection to interactions in which the inter-dye distance is less than ∼95 Å (which would yield an expected EFRET of ∼0.1).
evidence: This describes a limitation of the experimental system.

claim: The experiments have a 100 ms temporal resolution.
source: Additionally, our experiments have a 100 ms temporal resolution, and no binding would be detected, even if there was a FRET signal, if binding events had residence times much shorter than 100 ms.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the experimental system.

claim: No binding would be detected if binding events had residence times much shorter than 100 ms.
source: Additionally, our experiments have a 100 ms temporal resolution, and no binding would be detected, even if there was a FRET signal, if binding events had residence times much shorter than 100 ms.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the experimental system.

claim: The known SRP-RNC structures predict inter-dye distances of less than 50 Å.
source: Given that the known SRP-RNC structures predict inter-dye distances of less than 50 Å (Halic et al., 2006; Schaffitzel et al., 2006), and the shortest reported average residence time for an SRP-RNC binding event is ∼70–100 ms (Holtkamp et al., 2012), we are confident that we would detect binding events that are conformationally similar to the known SRP-RNC complexes.
evidence: This is based on structural data from prior studies.

claim: The shortest reported average residence time for an SRP-RNC binding event is approximately 70–100 ms.
source: Given that the known SRP-RNC structures predict inter-dye distances of less than 50 Å (Halic et al., 2006; Schaffitzel et al., 2006), and the shortest reported average residence time for an SRP-RNC binding event is ∼70–100 ms (Holtkamp et al., 2012), we are confident that we would detect binding events that are conformationally similar to the known SRP-RNC complexes.
evidence: This is based on prior kinetic measurements.

claim: Binding events that are conformationally similar to the known SRP-RNC complexes would be detected in this work.
source: Given that the known SRP-RNC structures predict inter-dye distances of less than 50 Å (Halic et al., 2006; Schaffitzel et al., 2006), and the shortest reported average residence time for an SRP-RNC binding event is ∼70–100 ms (Holtkamp et al., 2012), we are confident that we would detect binding events that are conformationally similar to the known SRP-RNC complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental parameters and prior structural/kinetic data.

claim: There may be intermediates in the binding reaction that would not be detected due to distance and temporal resolution limitations.
source: However, it is possible that there are intermediates in the binding reaction (including shot-lived, unproductive diffusional collision events) that we would not detect due to distance and temporal resolution limitations.
evidence: This acknowledges a potential limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: Such intermediates could be encounter complexes previously observed to form with approximately 10^6 M^−1 s^−1 association rates, regardless of nascent chain length.
source: Such intermediates could be encounter complexes previously observed to form with ∼106 M−1 s−1 association rates, regardless of nascent chain length (Holtkamp et al., 2012; Saraogi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation based on prior work.

claim: If such intermediates formed in the reaction, they would need to be conformationally distinct from known SRP-RNC structures, or they would have been detected in this work.
source: However, if such intermediates formed in our reaction, they would need to be conformationally distinct from known SRP-RNC structures, or they would have been detected in this work.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be required for undetected intermediates to exist.

claim: Discrepancies between current results and previous work may arise from differences between actively translating RNCs and stalled RNCs.
source: An alternative explanation for the discrepancies of our results to the previous work is that they may arise from differences between actively translating RNCs and stalled RNCs.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for differences between studies.

claim: When SRP binding events were compared among stalled RNCs, an enormous range in the variance of their arrival and residence times was observed (2.4–40.9 s and 0.4–58.7 s median arrival and residence times, respectively).
source: Our assays show that when SRP binding events were compared among stalled RNCs we observed an enormous range in the variance of their arrival and residence times (2.4–40.9 s and 0.4–58.7 s median arrival and residence times, respectively; Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The variability in stalled RNC binding kinetics indicates that individual stalled RNCs may exist in numerous different conformational states.
source: This variability indicates that individual stalled RNCs may exist in numerous different conformational states, many of which are likely to be inactive and perhaps off-pathway, despite each displaying the same length nascent chain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed variability in stalled RNC data.

claim: Many conformational states of stalled RNCs are likely to be inactive and perhaps off-pathway.
source: This variability indicates that individual stalled RNCs may exist in numerous different conformational states, many of which are likely to be inactive and perhaps off-pathway, despite each displaying the same length nascent chain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed variability in stalled RNC data.

claim: Quantitative results obtained with purified and stalled RNCs may be less physiologically relevant than results obtained with similarly purified but actively translating RNCs.
source: These data argue that quantitative results obtained with purified and stalled RNCs may be less physiologically relevant than results obtained with similarly purified but actively translating RNCs, which, by the very nature of the assay, represent functional states.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of stalled and actively translating RNCs.

claim: Actively translating RNCs, by the very nature of the assay, represent functional states.
source: These data argue that quantitative results obtained with purified and stalled RNCs may be less physiologically relevant than results obtained with similarly purified but actively translating RNCs, which, by the very nature of the assay, represent functional states.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the nature of actively translating RNCs.

claim: Studies in yeast and mammalian cells observed some preference of SRP for RNCs carrying a signal sequence before it was exposed from the ribosome.
source: Studies in yeast and mammalian cell observed some preference of SRP for RNCs carrying a signal sequence before it was exposed from the ribosome (Berndt et al., 2009; Mariappan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work in eukaryotic systems.

source: These studies used stalled RNCs in crude cell extracts, suggesting that perhaps factors absent in our assays and/or differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems might influence early SRP-RNC interactions and affect signal sequence discrimination.
evidence: This describes the methodology of prior eukaryotic studies.

claim: Factors absent in the current assays and/or differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems might influence early SRP-RNC interactions and affect signal sequence discrimination.

The calibration revealed that the observed signal corresponded to a corrected value of 0.33–0.5 EFRET (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, right panel).

source: This is lower than the expected EFRET of ∼0.85 predicted from molecular modeling onto cryo-EM structures of SRP bound to RNCs (Halic et al., 2006; Schaffitzel et al., 2006).

claim: The cryo-EM structures of SRP-RNC are relatively low resolution (9.6–16 Å).
source: However, these are relatively low resolution structures (9.6–16 Å), and our previous work has shown that SRP can take on a variety of conformations on the ribosome (Noriega et al., 2014), consistent with the observed bimodality in the EFRET distributions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

source: This assay allowed us to determine that stalled RNCs, despite being homogeneously stalled with a 55 amino acid nascent chain, show as much as 1–3 orders of magnitude differences in the median and variance of SRP arrival and residence times (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
